sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ògún** (*ogun*) — The Master of Iron — belongs to the Yoruba tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Iron, War, Labour". The name means "God of iron"[^1].

Ògún is the orisha of iron and of every road iron opens: the hunter who cleared the primordial forest so the gods could descend, the smith who arms the farmer and the warrior alike, and the patron of every worker who makes a living by metal — from the blacksmith to the surgeon to the driver.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Ògún** and serves its temple at [ògún.com](https://xn--gn-1ja7a.com). The restoration preserves the Yoruba tone marks — the grave on ò and the acute on ú — distinctive features the ASCII form loses, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *ogun* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.
William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.
Abraham, R. C., Dictionary of Modern Yoruba (London: University of London Press, 1958).

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Ògún** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "God of iron"[^1].

The ASCII form *ogun* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Ògún** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves the Yoruba tone marks — the grave on ò and the acute on ú — distinctive features the ASCII form loses, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **o** → **Ò** — Low tone (Yoruba)
- **g** → **g** — Same
- **u** → **ú** — High tone (Yoruba)
- **n** → **n** — Same

The project holds the domain **ògún.com** (xn--gn-1ja7a.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Abimbola.
Verger.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ò.gṹ/** — Yoruba.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: aw-GOON, low tone on the first syllable, high on the last.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Yoruba** — Ògún
- **Brazil** — Ogun / São Jorge
- **Haiti** — Ogou Feray
- **Owned form** — Ògún

Ògún carries Yoruba's tonal low-high melody: ò with the grave (low tone), gún with the acute (high) — the tones are phonemic, and the restoration keeps both exactly as the language requires. The name is bound to the word for iron (irin) in his praise-names: "Ògún, master of iron, the one who clears the road."

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual yoruba names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Ògún** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

Yoruba is written in Latin letters with tone marks — the orthography the restoration preserves: Ò (low tone) and ú (high tone) are the name as spoken. In the Ifá divination corpus his signs live in the odù Ogunda, "Ògún creates," one of the sixteen principal odù: the god written into the divination system itself.

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Ògún is the orisha of iron and of every road iron opens: the hunter who cleared the primordial forest so the gods could descend, the smith who arms the farmer and the warrior alike, and the patron of every worker who makes a living by metal — from the blacksmith to the surgeon to the driver.[^1]

### The Cutlass

His tool and emblem: the blade that clears the forest path — creation by cutting.

### The Forge

The smith's fire: iron is his body, and every smithy his shrine.

### The First Road

He hacked the road through the primal forest that let the orisha reach the earth.

### The Dog

His companion and sacrifice — the hunter's faithful one, honoured at his festivals.

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Ògún concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The cutlass** — The path-making blade — technology as the opener of ways
- **The anvil** — The forge's heart, where his power is hammered into tools
- **The palm wine** — His drink — offered by hunters and smiths for coolness and courage

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Ògún's myths are the Yoruba meditation on power: the strength that clears the way for everyone, and the rage that, unmastered, turns on its own town.[^1]

### The First Road (The Descent)

When the orisha first sought to descend to the earth, the primordial forest stood unbroken and none could pass — not Orunmila with his wisdom, not any god with any tool. Ògún took his cutlass and cut the road through, and the gods followed him down; for this he is saluted first in every rite, the opener of the way. Creation, in Yoruba thought, required not a word but a blade.[^2]

### The King of Ire (The Retreat)

Made king of the town of Ire, Ògún came one festival day to find the people silent — they did not greet him with the honours he was owed. In his rage he cut down his own people with the sword until his son stood in the way; coming to himself, he declared he would go no more among men, and sank into the earth — remaining, as his praise-songs say, in the iron itself. Every Ògún festival at Ire replays the king's coming and going.

### Master of the Forest (The Hunter)

Before he was king or smith, Ògún was the supreme hunter: lord of the deep forest where no farm grows, guide of the hunters' guilds whose odu-ifá praise-songs call him "the one who has water but bathes in blood." Hunters still chant his oríkì at the forest's edge: the road-opener is also the one who knows the road's dangers better than any god.

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.
Abraham, R. C., Dictionary of Modern Yoruba (London: University of London Press, 1958).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The Middle Passage carried him across the Atlantic, where the iron god found new irons: in Cuban Santería he is Oggún, syncretized with Saint Peter (keeper of the keys — the metal of heaven's gate) or Saint George; in Brazilian Candomblé, Ògún is Saint George of the dragon-slaying spear; in Haitian Vodou he is Ogou Feray, the warrior-loa of the forge and the soldier's flag. The saints changed the face; the iron, the road, and the dog kept the god.[^1]

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[anat|ꜥAnat]], [[ares|Árēs]], [[ashur|Aššur]], [[athena|Athénā]], [[durga|Durgā]], and [[huitzilopochtli|Huitzilopōchtli]], each linked through war / battle.

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Nigeria's Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka is his most famous devotee: Ògún is the patron of Soyinka's art — the road-maker who is also the destroyer — and the essay "The Fourth Stage" and the novel The Road are his modern liturgy. Ògún state in Nigeria bears his name; his praise-names echo in the foundries and mechanics' yards of every Yoruba city, where a splash of palm wine on the anvil still opens the working day.[^1]

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Yorubaland is one of Africa's oldest iron-working regions: the smelting furnaces of the Nsukka plateau (Lejja) date the craft back over two thousand years, and the guild-smithies of the forest belt kept the ritual side — the first iron of a furnace smelted with prayers to Ògún. His shrines are often the anvil itself; the great festivals of Ire and of Ọndó preserve the masquerades and the dog-sacrifice described in the earliest ethnographies, and the odù Ogunda verses are still divined daily by babaláwo across the Yoruba world.[^1]

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Ifá Corpus
sections.body: In the Ifá corpus Ògún's home is the odù **Ògúndá** — "Ògún creates" — one of the sixteen principal odù, whose verses tell the road-clearing, the rage, and the retreat, and whose divination clients are warned and promised in his terms: the blade that opens and the blade that wounds. Bascom's field record of Ifá divination shows the odù recited daily across Yorubaland, and the Ògún verses of the other odù (Ògúndá Méjì's tellings of the Ire kingship above all) make him one of the most-addressed orisha in the whole divination literature.

sources.citation: Bascom, Ifa Divination (Ògúndá verses); Idowu, Olodumare.

sections.label: Oral Tradition
sections.body:
The oríkì praise-names are his living titles, chanted at forge and forest's edge.

- **Ògún Onírè** — 'Ògún, Owner of Ire'; the town-king title, his civic name.
- **Ògún Aládà** — 'Owner of the Cutlass'; the blade as title.
- **Alágbẹ̀dẹ** — 'Master of the Smiths'; the guild-title of the iron-workers.
- **Ọ̀ṣìn imọ́lẹ̀** — 'the strong one who bathes in blood'; the hunter's praise-name.
- **Olójà onílù** — 'owner of the road and the town'; the paired domains, path and settlement.
- **Baba wa** — 'our father'; the devotees' everyday address.

sources.citation: Idowu, Olodumare (Ògún oriki); Bascom, Ifa Divination.

sections.label: Diaspora Traditions
sections.body: His sanctuaries are the working places of iron: at **Ire**, the town he ruled, his festival replays the king's coming and his withdrawal into the earth, and his shrine holds the ancient implements of the office. Every **smithy** in Yorubaland is his chapel — the anvil the altar, the first iron of the day offered with palm wine — and the hunters' guilds keep his forest shrines at the paths' entrances. In the diaspora, his altars stand in the Candomblé terreiros of Bahia and the Santería houses of Havana and Miami: the iron god's addresses follow the metal, as they always have.

sources.citation: Idowu, Olodumare; Bascom, Shango in the New World (Ògún cults).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Ògún is the god of the tool in the hand. Every technology is his: the blade that clears the road and the blade that clears the town are the same iron, and only the wielder's self-command decides which road it opens. He asks the maker's question, which is also the warrior's and the surgeon's: what does your strength serve — and who stands in the way when it slips?

Every driver who splashes gin on a bumper in Lagos, every mechanic who taps the anvil before the first weld, is keeping his liturgy without needing its name: tools are moral — they open roads or open wounds — and the hand must be steadier than the blade. Ògún's myth admits what no other war-god's does: that the rage is his own. The road-opener who cut down his own town is the honest patron of a technological age: the strength is real, the forest is real, and so is the apology owed when the blade turns.

Soyinka, his greatest modern devotee, calls him the god of the road and of transition — the patron of everyone who makes a path where none existed, and the warning that every path is cut through something. In the diaspora's forge-altars the lesson survives translation: iron does not apologize, but it must be answered for. The road-opener asks of every builder, coder, and driver the same question his own myth could not escape: when the forest is cleared, what will you plant — and whom did the clearing cost?

The anvil rings, the day's first iron is cut, and the road — his road — opens another meter. The forest always grows back; that is why the clearing is a daily act, and why the god of the cutlass is worshipped not once but every working morning.[^1]

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.
